summary: This experimental document describes a way to measure packet loss, delay and jitter on live traffic using alternate marking, a coloring technique. It includes a report showing an example and where the method applies. It was replaced by RFC 9341.

eli5.summary: Packets are painted red or blue in alternating batches. By counting each color at two points, you can see how many went missing and how long they took.

subtitle: Measure packet loss, delay, and jitter on live traffic using packet coloring and counting.

tldr.problem: Service providers need accurate ways to measure packet loss, delay, and jitter on live production traffic to ensure quality of experience. Traditional methods either inject probe packets (active measurement) which load the network, or require complex sequence numbering that is hard to implement at line rate.
tldr.mechanism: The Alternate-Marking method colors packets alternately (e.g., red and blue) in time-based blocks. By counting packets of each color at different points in the network, operators can calculate packet loss with single-packet granularity. Timestamps on marked packets measure delay; repeated samples give jitter statistics.
tldr.outcome: This experimental technique allows passive performance monitoring without probe packets, deployed successfully in production networks. It was later refined into RFC 9341 as a standards-track specification. The method works on any packet-based traffic (Ethernet, IP, MPLS) with minimal performance impact.

facts.label: Applicable traffic types
facts.value: Ethernet, IP, MPLS, unicast and multicast

facts.label: Time synchronization needed
facts.value: Yes; NTP or PTP depending on required precision

today: RFC 8321 is an Experimental specification from January 2018 and has been obsoleted by RFC 9341, which provides a standards-track update while preserving the core methods. The Alternate-Marking technique is deployed in production networks and has proven to be a practical and accurate approach for passive performance monitoring on live traffic.

sections.title: The Challenge of Measuring Live Traffic
sections.content:
Service providers carry traffic with strict quality requirements: video, voice, and real-time applications are sensitive to packet loss, delay, and jitter (variation in delay). Monitoring these metrics accurately is essential for network management and quality assurance.

Traditional measurement approaches have limitations: active measurement (sending probe packets) adds artificial traffic; sequence numbering requires extracting and processing header fields at line rate, which is complex and expensive. This RFC proposes Alternate Marking, a simple method for passive measurement on live traffic, requiring no probe packets and working with existing network hardware capabilities.
sections.eli5: To know if your internet is working well, you need to measure how many packets get lost, how long they take to arrive, and if the timing is steady. But doing this without slowing down the network is hard. This RFC describes an easy way to do it.

sections.title: The Alternate-Marking Method
sections.content:
The core idea is simple: divide a traffic flow into consecutive blocks by alternately coloring packets with two values (A and B). Each block contains packets of one color; when the color switches, the block ends and a new one begins. Routers count packets of each color on each interface.

By comparing counters from two routers, the difference reveals packet loss in that segment. For example, if Router 1 sends 1000 A-colored packets and Router 2 receives 995, then 5 packets were lost between them. This provides single-packet granularity without needing to track individual packet identity.

The coloring can be done by changing an existing field (like the DSCP field) or using a dedicated marking field. Color switches can be triggered by a timer (preferable for consistency) or after a fixed packet count. Routers need only two counters per flow per interface—one for color A, one for color B—a minimal addition to existing functionality.
sections.eli5: Split the packet stream into batches by color: red packets, then blue packets, alternating. Each router watches its interfaces and counts how many red and blue packets pass through. To measure loss between two points, compare the counts: the difference is how many packets didn't make it.

sections.title: Measuring Loss, Delay, and Jitter
sections.content:
Packet Loss Measurement: Count A-colored and B-colored packets at the ingress and egress of a link. When a block ends (color switches), compare the two counters. If 100 packets of color A entered but only 95 exited, 5 were lost.

Delay Measurement: Use the color change as a time reference. A router records the timestamp of the first packet of each color block and compares it with the timestamp of the same packet at another router. The difference is the one-way delay. For robustness against packet loss and reordering, the method can use mean delay (average arrival time of all packets in a block) rather than tracking individual packets.

Jitter Measurement: Delay variation is derived from consecutive delay samples. By taking multiple delay measurements within blocks, statistics like percentiles and variance can be calculated. A double-marking approach uses a second level of marking to select specific packets within each color block for precise per-packet delay measurement, giving detailed statistics without measuring every packet.
sections.eli5: Loss is easy: count the colors in and out. Delay needs timestamps: mark when a red packet leaves one router and compare to when it arrives at the next. Jitter is how much the delay varies. For detailed statistics, mark special packets within each color batch to measure them precisely.

sections.title: Implementation and Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
Synchronization: Routers must be synchronized to a common time reference with accuracy of +/- (A/2), where A is the acceptable clock error. The color block duration L must be large enough that L > 2d, where d accounts for clock error and network delay variation. Practical choices often range from seconds to minutes depending on desired measurement frequency and clock accuracy.

Flow Identification: Implementations can use two strategies. Flow-based monitoring applies coloring to specific traffic flows (identified by header matching rules), requiring knowledge of flow paths. Link-based monitoring colors all traffic on a link, measuring link-wide statistics without needing to track individual flows. Link-based is simpler and more robust to traffic engineering changes.

Counter Management: When should counters be read? If colors switch on a timer, read the A-colored counter after the A block ends (when color B is active) and vice versa, waiting L/2 after the color switch to account for out-of-order packets. The RFC specifies mechanisms for both centralized collection (via SNMP or FTP to a management system) and distributed bilateral exchange between endpoints.
sections.eli5: Routers need synchronized clocks so they agree on which packets are red and which are blue. Color blocks should last long enough that delays and timing errors don't cause confusion. Read the counters carefully, waiting for reordered packets to arrive. A management system collects the counts and calculates the loss.

sections.title: Operational Deployment and Applicability
sections.content:
The Alternate-Marking method has been experimentally deployed in production networks by major service providers. The technique requires only features available on current routing platforms: interface counters that can be filtered by packet fields, and synchronized time (NTP or PTP). Hardware implementations are straightforward; software can also apply the method.

The method works on any packet-based or frame-based traffic—Ethernet, IP, MPLS—and supports both unicast and multicast. Measurement accuracy is excellent: single-packet granularity for loss, and timestamp precision depends on the time synchronization mechanism chosen (NTP for millisecond accuracy, PTP for microsecond). The method is robust to packet reordering and does not introduce artificial load on the network.

This is an Experimental specification that is used in production. It was later standardized as RFC 9341, which provides an updated standards-track definition while maintaining the core concepts and methods described here.
sections.eli5: This method works in real networks today. It requires features routers already have, doesn't slow down traffic, and works on any type of packet. It was later made a proper standard (RFC 9341) but the basic idea stays the same.
